Yes - Roundabout has some great Rick Wakeman keyboard work for the last third of the song, and Christopher Squire's bass sound has always been a favorite of mine. However, Yes was generally a little too "out there" for the main stream rock world. But for intricate stuff from them, Roundabout, Starship Trooper, Yours Is No Disgrace, And You and I... if you make it as far as "Owner of a Lonely Heart," you went too far, turn around and go back!

Allman Brothers - Jessica, Melissa, Midnight Rider, Whipping Post, and on and on. (And, SoulShine is always worth a listen!)

Foghat's "Slow Ride" is always good for scratching that itch, but I generally get tired of it if I hear it more than once a year or so (Got burned out on it when it came out, I guess!) Great bass riff through the bridge, though!

Janis Joplin / Big Brother "Me and Bobby McGee" has a great high-speed ending that isn't exactly rock, but certainly worth a listen!

Genesis... I have to include them in a list like this, not because they were big rockers, but because they had some fantastic keyboards and drums on the few songs where they really cut loose - Cinema Show, Firth of Fifth, One For the Vine - these are some fairly mellow songs that have a huge loud fast complex bit that shows up unannounced, but always remind me of the "wow" factor these guys had (before "Abacab" signaled the end of their era.)

Rush's La Villa Strangiato was relatively unheard since it was released, but is, imho, required listening for anyone wanting to explore their genius... the high-hat riff that lasts through most of the song is enough to make my wrists hurt. (There's a version of it live that dispels any rumours of pre-recorded drum tracks, but I still prefer the studio version.)

Robin Trower's "Two Rolling Stoned" has a great guitar-fueled bluesy sound, just be careful listening to it while driving - I tend to hit about 90 without ever realizing it!
